title: MailEx: Email Event and Argument Extraction
abstract: Introduces MailEx, an event-extraction dataset built from conversational email threads with a taxonomy of 10 event types and 76 argument roles. The dataset contains roughly 1.5K threads, 4K emails, and 8K event instances, and exposes challenges including non-contiguous or shared triggers, non-named-entity arguments, and dependence on conversational history.

title: MAVEN-ARG: Completing the Puzzle of All-in-One Event Understanding Dataset with Event Argument Annotation
abstract: Extends MAVEN with exhaustive document-level event-argument annotations, creating an integrated benchmark for event detection, argument extraction, and event relations. It covers 162 event types, 612 argument roles, 98,591 events, and 290,613 entity and non-entity arguments.

title: Multi-Sentence Argument Linking
abstract: Introduces RAMS and a document-level model for finding argument spans that fill event roles across sentence boundaries. RAMS contains 9,124 annotated events spanning 139 event types and directly evaluates cross-sentence argument linking.

title: Document-Level Event Argument Extraction by Conditional Generation
abstract: Formulates document-level event argument extraction as conditional generation and introduces WikiEvents with complete event and coreference annotation. It also evaluates informative argument extraction, a harder setting requiring implicit coreference reasoning to recover useful argument mentions.

title: Document-Level Event Role Filler Extraction using Multi-Granularity Contextualized Encoding
abstract: Studies document-level event role-filler extraction where evidence needed for an argument can occur across multiple sentences. The model identifies textual spans for event roles using context represented at multiple granularities and is evaluated on MUC-4.

title: A Two-Stream AMR-enhanced Model for Document-level Event Argument Extraction
abstract: Targets long-distance document-level event arguments using local and global AMR representations. Its auxiliary boundary loss explicitly models argument-span boundaries, and experiments use RAMS and WikiEvents.

title: Textual Entailment for Event Argument Extraction: Zero- and Few-Shot with Multi-Source Learning
abstract: Recasts event argument extraction as textual entailment and evaluates transfer between ACE and WikiEvents. The method reduces dependence on a single event schema and provides evidence for transferring structured argument extraction across domains with limited target annotation.

title: EA²E: Improving Consistency with Event Awareness for Document-Level Argument Extraction
abstract: Models consistency of a participant's argument roles across multiple related events in the same document. The Event-Aware Argument Extraction model uses event-event context and is evaluated on WikiEvents and ACE2005, making it relevant to multi-action ownership and role consistency.

title: BEMEAE: Moving Beyond Exact Span Match for Event Argument Extraction
abstract: Examines limitations of exact-span-match evaluation for event argument extraction by evaluating nine models on RAMS and GENEVA. It introduces BEMEAE, which supplements deterministic matching with semantic equivalence and is reported to align more closely with human judgments, making the paper useful for designing evidence-span evaluation protocols.

title: MUC-4 Revisited: Document-level Event Analysis beyond Span-based Arguments
abstract: Revisits the full original MUC-4 task rather than only its commonly used span-extraction subset. The formulation combines textual arguments with normalized, inferred, and categorical event information such as actor identities, temporal scope, and aggregated outcomes, and evaluates generative document-level models.

title: Enhancing Document-level Event Argument Extraction with Contextual Clues and Role Relevance
abstract: Introduces a document-level event argument extraction model that uses non-argument contextual clues and dependencies among argument roles. Its span-trigger contextual pooling explicitly relates candidate argument spans to event triggers and is evaluated on RAMS and WikiEvents.

title: Semantic Role Labeling of Implicit Arguments for Nominal Predicates
abstract: Introduces a manually annotated corpus of implicit arguments for ten NomBank predicates and studies automatic recovery of arguments that are absent from the predicate's local syntactic context. The work provides direct empirical methodology for discourse-context recovery of omitted semantic participants.

title: Inducing Implicit Arguments from Comparable Texts: A Framework and Its Applications
abstract: Develops a framework for inducing implicit semantic arguments from comparable texts and applies it to implicit argument processing. It provides transferable mechanisms for recovering participants that are not overtly expressed with the predicate.

title: Combining Seemingly Incompatible Corpora for Implicit Semantic Role Labeling
abstract: Studies how differently annotated resources can be combined for implicit semantic role labeling. The paper is relevant to owner recovery because the target roles may need to be resolved from discourse rather than from an overt sentence-local argument.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Prototypical Fillers for Implicit Semantic Role Labeling
abstract: Investigates unsupervised learning of prototypical role fillers for implicit semantic role labeling. It offers a transferable approach for predicting semantically expected participants when arguments are omitted from the immediate predicate context.

title: Implicit Argument Prediction with Event Knowledge
abstract: Addresses prediction of implicit arguments that are not syntactically connected to their predicates. The approach incorporates event knowledge, narrative coherence, and entity salience and is evaluated on both synthetic and naturally occurring implicit arguments.

title: A Multi-Axis Annotation Scheme for Event Temporal Relations
abstract: Proposes a multi-axis scheme for annotating temporal relations among events and simplifies relation judgments by focusing on event start points. The resulting MATRES-style annotation methodology is transferable to explicit action-to-time relation annotation rather than proximity-based date assignment.

title: An Annotation Framework for Dense Event Ordering
abstract: Introduces TimeBank-Dense, an annotation framework designed to produce densely connected event temporal graphs rather than sparse selected relations. Dense pairwise annotation provides a useful methodological precedent for evaluating whether temporal expressions and events are attached to the correct target rather than inferred locally.

title: Dense Event Ordering with a Multi-Pass Architecture
abstract: Studies temporal ordering over densely connected event graphs and introduces a sieve architecture in which earlier high-precision temporal decisions constrain later ones through transitive closure. It provides transfer evidence for globally consistent temporal binding when many events coexist in a document.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics

title: A Structured Learning Approach to Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Treats event temporal relation extraction as a structured prediction problem in which relations among other events constrain a target pair. The approach directly addresses global consistency and missing relations, properties relevant to binding a time expression or deadline to the correct action among several actions.

title: TDDiscourse: A Dataset for Discourse-Level Temporal Ordering of Events
abstract: Extends TimeBank-Dense with manually annotated temporal relations between events separated by more than one sentence. The benchmark specifically targets document-level temporal reasoning where local syntactic proximity is insufficient.

title: TORQUE: A Reading Comprehension Dataset of Temporal Ordering Questions
abstract: Introduces a temporal-reasoning benchmark whose questions require determining relationships among events, including relations not stated explicitly. It provides transfer evidence for contextual temporal reasoning rather than assigning times solely from surface proximity.

title: TIMERS: Document-level Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Addresses document-level temporal relation extraction using discourse, semantic-role, and contextual information. It is evaluated on temporal-relation benchmarks including TDDiscourse, TimeBank-Dense, and MATRES and is relevant to long-range temporal attachment among multiple events.

title: Utilizing Relative Event Time to Enhance Event-Event Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Jointly models event-event temporal relations and an auxiliary relative-event-time prediction task. The paper explicitly notes the sparsity of event-to-time links in TimeBank-Dense and evaluates whether inferred event times improve temporal relation classification.

title: SemEval-2015 Task 6: Clinical TempEval
abstract: Defines a shared evaluation for extraction of temporal information in clinical narratives, including events, time expressions, and temporal relations. Although domain-specific to clinical text, its relation tasks provide transferable empirical machinery for evaluating event-to-time attachment rather than time-expression recognition alone.

title: FactBank: a corpus annotated with event factuality
abstract: Adds event-factuality annotations to TimeBank, representing whether mentioned events are presented as actual, non-occurring, or uncertain. The corpus is designed around the interaction of multiple linguistic factuality markers and provides transfer evidence for distinguishing asserted actions from negated, uncertain, or otherwise non-factual events.

title: Modality and Negation in Event Extraction
abstract: Presents an event extraction system that explicitly represents multiple kinds of modality and negation so that non-actual events are not treated as ordinary factual events. Its political-news setting makes it transfer rather than workplace evidence, but it directly connects modality information to extracted events.

title: Agent-Specific Deontic Modality Detection in Legal Language
abstract: Introduces LEXDEMOD, an English-contract corpus in which deontic modality is annotated relative to a specific contracting party or agent together with modal trigger spans. It benchmarks both agent-specific multi-label modality classification and joint agent-specific modality and trigger-span detection, directly separating deontic meanings instead of collapsing all modality.

title: Reading between the Lines: Information Extraction from Industry Requirements
abstract: Defines each natural-language industry requirement in terms of scope, condition, and demand and introduces sequence-labeling and few-shot baselines for extracting those semantic components. The paper identifies implicit scope as a major challenge and shows that document context helps its recovery, making it particularly relevant to condition attachment and omitted arguments.

title: Computable Contracts by Extracting Obligation Logic Graphs
abstract: Explores extraction of obligation logic graphs from natural-language contracts to support computable representations of obligations. The work includes modeling of complex conditions, making it transferable to structured action-plus-condition extraction even though the source domain is legal rather than workplace communication.

title: Towards Generative Event Factuality Prediction
abstract: Introduces an end-to-end generative formulation for jointly predicting factuality holders, factuality targets, and factuality values. Experiments use all sources and targets represented in FactBank, providing transferable evidence for attaching factuality or modality-like status to the correct proposition and holder rather than assigning a sentence-level label.

title: Summarizing Decisions in Spoken Meetings
abstract: Studies generation of a concise decision abstract for each decision in a spoken meeting using token-level and dialogue-act-level methods. Because it targets the content of individual decisions rather than merely labeling a meeting as decision-related, it provides transfer evidence for extracting decision propositions, although the source is spoken meetings rather than email or enterprise chat.
venue: Workshop on Automatic Summarization for Different Genres, Media, and Languages

title: Unsupervised Topic Modeling Approaches to Decision Summarization in Spoken Meetings
abstract: Presents token-level decision summarization methods that identify summary-worthy words in meeting decision discussions using fine-grained topic models and contextual information. The work provides transfer evidence for recovering the substantive content of a decision rather than only detecting a decision-related dialogue region.
